title: Public header links disappear against a white navigation bar
customer: Any first-time desktop visitor trying to find plans, modules, examples or login.
consequence: People can miss the primary information links and believe the navigation is empty. The dark launch-partner CTA remains usable.
reproduction: Open /platform/promo at 1440 px in Chromium or WebKit, or Safari desktop. Read computed styles for .eb-studio-nav and its ordinary anchors.
observed: Foreground and background are both rgb(255,255,255), giving 1:1 contrast. Safari visual inspection confirms effectively invisible links/logo. The existing interaction tests pass because visibility/role assertions do not assert readable contrast. Lighthouse also flags a separate workflow-button contrast of 3.58:1.
expected: All shown navigation labels remain legible and meet the applicable contrast threshold in default, hover and focus states.
cause: Confirmed CSS name collision: Marketing Desk globally reuses .eb-studio-nav with background:white after public-studio.css has set white foreground.
confidence: High; reproduced live and locally in two engines, plus Safari.
remedy: Scope or rename Marketing Desk selectors; preserve the intended public header theme; add a meaningful cross-surface contrast regression.

title: Public package and Messaging price descriptions disagree
customer: An owner comparing Starter, Growth, Pro and messaging costs.
consequence: A buyer cannot reliably decide what the quoted plan includes or what Messaging costs; staff must explain conflicting pages.
reproduction: Compare /platform/start with /platform/plans, then compare Messaging in /explore/modules with the Messaging add-on card.
observed: The start comparison describes Starter as including everything while plans reserve loyalty/birthdays and wishlist for higher tiers. Messaging shows $19.99/month on plans and $99/month plus $99 setup in Explorer. The first-six-month Launch Partner offer is internally consistent on current live pages; the older checkout has different historical post-introductory terms.
expected: The same product has one unambiguous inclusion and price explanation, with bundle distinctions made explicit.
cause: Confirmed separate display/config paths; modulePurchaseMetadata returns the first add-on containing a module, which selects SMS before the standalone Messaging add-on. The Starter wording conflict is a separate duplicated content problem.
confidence: High for mismatch and source mechanism. No actual mischarge was tested or alleged.
remedy: Use an explicit canonical purchase identity for standalone Messaging versus the SMS bundle and derive comparison wording from the catalog. Preserve every current price and accepted agreement.

title: Plans and intake expose internal, placeholder and legacy add-ons
customer: A new owner selecting requested capabilities.
consequence: Customers can request obsolete or internal options without understanding whether they exist or can be supplied. This increases manual triage and contradicts the safe public catalog.
reproduction: Open plans and expand the commercial interests on start. Compare AI Branch, aliases and future products with the canonical public/internal catalog.
observed: AI Branch Starter/Growth/Pro appear publicly despite INTERNAL_ONLY module state. Legacy aliases and placeholder options are listed. The plans page can simultaneously claim no coming-soon modules are exposed while showing coming-soon add-on pills.
expected: A single public visibility/purchase policy filters cards and interest inputs; roadmap interest, if intentionally offered later, is a distinct explicit product decision.
cause: publicPlansPayload enumerates compatibility add-ons without the Explorer policy, and its options are reused in intake.
confidence: High. This is choice exposure; automatic entitlement activation, charging or data exposure was not demonstrated.
remedy: Apply fail-closed catalog visibility and canonical identity filtering to plans, option rendering and submitted interest validation; retain aliases internally.

title: Electrician prospects are filtered out with a hidden tutorial
customer: Tradespeople whose business is an electrical contractor.
consequence: A currently demonstrated audience cannot accurately choose its business type during public intake; Other is a workaround.
reproduction: Inspect public start business types. Run PlatformPlansAndAccessRequestsTest with the default customer_electrician_tutorial flag off. Compare the supported post-login electrician workspace setup.
observed: Electrician is absent and a submitted electrician key is rejected. The post-login wizard and field workspace support it.
expected: Industry selection follows supported customer types independently of whether an optional customer tutorial is enabled.
cause: filteredPublicBusinessTypes couples industry availability to features.customer_electrician_tutorial.
confidence: High for local render/validation and source. A production submission was intentionally not made.
remedy: Separate industry eligibility from tutorial rollout; keep the tutorial hidden and add a focused field-prospect intake test.

title: Failed integration-health reads look like zero open issues
customer: Staff responsible for noticing delayed imports and integration failures.
consequence: A failing probe can look clean, delaying investigation and producing a misleading quality report.
reproduction: In a disposable in-memory database without integration_health_events, bootstrap the application and call OperationalStatusService::openIssues. Trace the returned value to the developer view.
observed: The aggregator rescues read exceptions into total=0, empty severity and recent lists, with no known/error marker. The view renders the number as Integration health.
expected: A failed probe displays unknown/unavailable, with safe diagnostic evidence and a last-success timestamp when available.
cause: rescue fallback values encode legitimate zero data rather than an explicit failed observation.
confidence: High for reproduced local failure semantics. Production database failure was not observed.
remedy: Return a typed known/unknown status and display it truthfully; include a fault-injection verification for the aggregator and view.

title: Current setup guidance competes with historical doctrine and technical copy
customer: Prospective owners, newly approved users and future maintainers.
consequence: Buyers do not get one clear request-to-first-value explanation, and maintainers can mistake old readiness/ownership claims for present rules.
reproduction: Read the current public plans/start copy and its tests, then compare the dated master readiness document and README_FOR_AGENTS with October first-workspace/mobile code and public company branding.
observed: Plans uses implementation language about deferred billing writes. The start tests explicitly exclude a what-happens-next explanation. May readiness claims and old Fire Forge Tech ownership text coexist with October capabilities and Evergrove branding. Current documents span thousands of lines with multiple dated release assertions.
expected: One short current product/setup map distinguishes request, approval, login, setup and first useful task; historical documents remain clearly historical.
cause: Accumulated release notes and parallel public/technical descriptions without a single maintained current entry point.
confidence: High for the conflicting text; no assumption that historical documents describe current production failure.
remedy: Add concise current guidance and mark historical readiness sections by scope/date; replace implementation language on customer pages without rewriting legal or historical evidence.
